Surah Hud, peace be upon him, is Meccan and has one hundred and twenty-three verses.

In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. A Book⦆ meaning: this is a Book, so it is the predicate of an omitted subject (mubtada'). ﴿Whose verses have been made firm⦆ is a description of it, meaning: they have been arranged in a sound, firm composition, free of any deficiency or defect, like a well-built structure. ﴿Then have been detailed⦆ as pearls are set apart in necklaces by jewels, [detailed] with the proofs of divine oneness, the rulings, the admonitions and the narratives. Or it means they were made into sections, surah by surah and verse by verse. Or it means they were revealed in parts and not sent down all at once. Or it means that in it is set out what the worshipper needs, that is, it was made clear and summarized. The meaning of "then" (thumma) here is not delay in time but rather delay in status. ﴿From the presence of One who is All-Wise, All-Aware⦆ is another description of "a Book," or a second predicate, or a complement to "have been made firm" and "have been detailed," meaning: its rulings and its detailing come from Him.

﴿Alla ta'budu illa Allah﴾ is a maf'ul lahu (object of purpose), meaning: "so that you do not worship except Allah." Or it is an explanatory (mufassira) "an" (that), because in the detailing of the verses there is the sense of speech, as if it were said: "He said: do not worship except Allah," or "He commanded you that you not worship except Allah." ﴿Verily I am to you from Him a warner and a bringer of good tidings﴾, i.e., from Allah.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verse 3:

﴿And that you seek forgiveness from your Lord﴾ i.e., He has commanded you to affirm the Oneness (tawhid) and to seek forgiveness. ﴿Then turn to Him in repentance﴾ i.e., seek His forgiveness for shirk, then return to Him through obedience. ﴿He will let you enjoy a good provision﴾ He will prolong your benefit in this world with good and pleasing benefits, of a wide livelihood and continuous blessings. ﴿Until a specified term﴾ until He takes you in death. ﴿And He will give every person of virtue his virtue﴾ and in the Hereafter He will give everyone who had virtue in knowledge, and an increase in it, the reward of his virtue, without diminishing anything from it. ﴿But if you turn away﴾ (p-47) and if you should turn away ﴿then indeed I fear for you the punishment of a great day﴾, which is the Day of Resurrection.
﴿To Allah is your return﴾: your returning (to Him). ﴿And He is Powerful over all things﴾: so He is able to restore you.

Verily they fold up their breasts (ألا إنَّهم يَثْنُونَ صُدُورَهُمْ): they turn away from the truth and deviate from it, because whoever turns toward a thing faces it with his breast, and whoever turns away from it and deviates bends his breast away from it and folds his side away from it. (لِيَسْتَخْفُوا مِنهُ) "That they may hide themselves from Him": that they may seek concealment from Allah, so that His Messenger and the believers will not perceive their turning away. (ألا حِينَ يَسْتَغْشُونَ ثِيابَهُمْ) "Unquestionably, when they wrap themselves in their garments": they cover themselves with them, i.e., they wish to conceal themselves when they wrap themselves in their garments, out of aversion to hearing the words of Allah, like the saying of Noah, peace be upon him: ﴿They put their fingers in their ears and wrapped themselves in their garments﴾ [Nuh: 7]. (يَعْلَمُ ما يُسِرُّونَ وما يُعْلِنُونَ) "He knows what they conceal and what they disclose": i.e., there is no difference in His knowledge between their concealing and their disclosing, so there is no way for them to achieve what they desire of concealment. Allah is aware of their folding of their breasts and their wrapping of their garments, and their hypocrisy is not concealed from Him. It was said: it was revealed concerning the hypocrites. (إنَّهُ عَلِيمٌ بِذاتِ الصُدُورِ) "Indeed, He is Knower of what is within the breasts": of what is in them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verse 6:

﴿And there is no creature on the earth but that upon Allah is its provision﴾ as a bounty (tafaddul), not as an obligation (wujub). ﴿And He knows its place of residence﴾ its location on the earth and its dwelling, ﴿and its place of storage﴾ where it was deposited before settling, from a loin (sulb), or a womb (rahim), or an egg, ﴿all of it is in a clear register﴾ each one of the creatures (dawabb), its provision, its place of residence and its place of storage, is in the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh), meaning: its mention is written in it, made clear.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verse 7:

﴿It is He who created the heavens and the earth﴾ and what is between them ﴿in six days﴾, from Sunday (al-Ahad) to Friday (al-Jumu'ah), as a teaching in deliberateness (ta'anni). ﴿And His Throne was upon the water﴾, i.e., above it. He means that beneath it there was no creation before the creation of the heavens and the earth except water. In this there is evidence that the Throne and the water were created before the creation of the heavens and the earth. It is said that He began by creating a green ruby (yaqut), and He looked at it in awe, so it turned into water. Then He created wind, which held the water on its back, and then He placed His Throne upon the water. In the Throne's standing upon the water there is a very great lesson for people of reflection. ﴿That He may test you﴾, i.e., He created the heavens and the earth and what is between them as a place of trial for those who are tested therein, and He did not create these things for their own sake. ﴿Which of you is best in deed﴾, i.e., most grateful. And from him (peace be upon him) [it is reported]: "Best in intellect, most scrupulous regarding the prohibitions of Allah, and quickest in obedience to Allah. Whoever gives thanks and obeys, He rewards him, and whoever disbelieves and disobeys, He punishes him." Since this resembles the testing of one who tests, He said "that He may test you", i.e., that He may do to you what the one who tests does to discover your conditions: how you act. ﴿And if you, [O Muhammad], say, "Indeed, you will be resurrected after death," those who disbelieve will surely say﴾ ﴿"This is not but obvious magic."﴾ By "this" he refers to the Qur'an, because the Qur'an is what speaks of the resurrection; when they call it magic, the denial of what it contains of resurrection and other matters is included within that. "Sahir" (magic) is read by Hamzah and Ali, meaning other than the Messenger. And the magician is a liar, a nullifier (of truth).

﴿And if We delay the punishment from them﴾, the punishment of the Hereafter or the punishment of the Day of Badr, ﴿until a community﴾, meaning until a group of periods of time, ﴿numbered﴾, meaning known, or a few. The meaning is until a known time. ﴿They will surely say, "What holds it back?"﴾, meaning what prevents it from descending, hastening for it in a manner of denial and mockery. ﴿Unquestionably, on the day it comes to them﴾, the punishment, ﴿it will not be averted from them﴾, the punishment will not be averted from them. "Yawma" (on the day) is in the accusative and is governed by "maṣrūfan" (averted), meaning: the punishment will not be averted from them on the day it comes to them. ﴿And there will surround them﴾, and encompass them, ﴿what they used to mock﴾, the punishment which they used to hasten for. "Yastahzi'ūn" (they mock) was used in place of "yasta'jilūn" (they hasten), because their hastening was in the manner of mockery.

(p-49)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verse 9:

﴿And if We let man taste mercy from Us﴾ — the definite article here is for the genus (lil-jins), meaning mankind in general — ﴿mercy﴾ — a blessing of health, security and wealth — and the lam in "la'in" (la'in, "if indeed") is the lam of tawti'at al-qasam (the lam that prepares the ground for an oath). ﴿Then We withdraw it from him﴾ — then We deprive him of that blessing — and the answer to the oath is ﴿he is truly despairing﴾ — intensely hopeless that the like of that stripped blessing will return to him, cutting off his hope in the vastness of Allah's bounty, without patience or submission to His decree — ﴿ungrateful﴾ — greatly ungrateful for what had passed for him of fluctuating in the blessing of Allah, forgetting it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verse 10:

﴿And if We let him taste ease after hardship had touched him﴾ — We broadened the blessing upon him after the poverty that had befallen him. ﴿He will surely say, "The evils have gone away from me,"﴾ — that is, the calamities that distressed me. ﴿Indeed, he is exultant and boastful﴾ — exulting (ashir) and insolent (bathir). ﴿Proud and boastful﴾ — over the people, because of the blessings Allah has let him taste. The exultation and boasting have preoccupied him from giving thanks.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verse 11:

﴿Except those who are patient﴾ in the trial and affliction, ﴿and do righteous deeds﴾ and give thanks in blessing and ease. ﴿For them is forgiveness﴾ for their sins, ﴿and a great reward﴾, meaning Paradise.

They used to propose to him signs out of obstinacy, not in search of guidance, for if they had been seeking guidance, one sign from what he brought would have been sufficient for their rightly guided course, and [it would have been sufficient] among their proposals. ﴿Why has no treasure been sent down to him, or an angel come with him?﴾ They did not value the Qur'an and held it in contempt, so the chest of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would constrict at conveying to them what they would not accept and at which they would laugh. So He spurred him on to discharge the message and to cast off concern for their rejection, their mockery, and their proposals, by His saying: ﴿So perhaps you will leave aside some of what is revealed to you﴾, i.e., perhaps you will leave off conveying it to them and delivering it to them out of fear of their rejection of it and their contempt for it. ﴿And your breast is constricted by it﴾, that you would recite it to them. He did not say "ḍayyiq" (constricted) so as to indicate that it is a passing constriction that is not lasting, because he, peace be upon him, was the most expansive of people in breast, and because it fits better with "tārik" (one who leaves aside). ﴿Lest they say﴾: out of fear that they would say, ﴿Why has no treasure been sent down to him, or an angel come with him?﴾ Why was not sent down to him what we have requested of the treasure, so that we might spend it, and the angels, so that we might affirm him? And why was there sent down to him what we do not want and do not propose? ﴿You are only a warner﴾, i.e., it is incumbent upon you only to warn them with what has been revealed to you and to convey to them what you have been commanded to convey; it is not incumbent upon you whether they reject or disregard it. ﴿And Allah is Guardian over all things﴾: He watches over what they say, and He will deal with them as is required; so rely upon Him, entrust your affair to Him, and devote yourself to conveying the revelation with an expansive heart and an open breast, not turning toward their arrogance nor heeding their foolishness and mockery.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verse 13:

﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"?﴾ "Am" here is *munqati'ah* (disconnected, introducing a fresh question). "Its pronoun" refers to what is revealed to you. ﴿Say: "Then bring ten surahs"﴾. He first challenged them with ten surahs, then with a single surah, like the one who says to his companion in writing, "Write ten lines similar to what I write." When it becomes clear to him that he cannot do so, he says, "I have settled for one line from you." ﴿Like it﴾ in beauty and eloquence (*jazalah*). The meaning of "like it" is "its likes," with regard to each one of them being similar to it. ﴿Forged﴾ is an attribute of "ten surahs." When they said, "You have invented the Qur'an and fabricated it from yourself, and it is not from God," He let them run with the reins and said, "Suppose I fabricated it from my own self. Then you too bring a speech like it, fabricated from your own selves, for you are eloquent Arabs like me." ﴿And call upon whomever you can besides God﴾ to help you in the counter-challenge. ﴿If you are truthful﴾ that it is forged.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verse 14:**

﴿So if they do not respond to you, then know that it has been revealed with the knowledge of God, and that there is no god but Him.﴾ That is: it was revealed containing what none but God knows, namely an inimitable composition (*nazm*) that is beyond the capacity of creation, and reports of unseen matters to which they have no access. "And" know at that time "that there is no god but God" alone, that His oneness is obligatory, and that associating partners with Him (*shirk*) is a great wrong. The address was made plural after being singular, namely in "you" (*lakum*) and "know" (*fa-'lamu*) after the words "Say" (*qul*), either because the plural is to honour the Messenger of God (ﷺ), or because the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and the believers used to address them, or because the address is to the polytheists. The pronoun in "they do not respond" (*lam yastajibu*) refers to those whom you invoke, meaning: if those whom you call upon besides God do not respond to you by supporting you in producing the like of it, because they know their incapacity to do so, then know that it was revealed "with the knowledge of God," that is, with His permission or by His command. ﴿Will you then submit?﴾ That is, will you follow Islam after this decisive proof? And whoever makes the address to the Muslims, its meaning is: remain steadfast upon the knowledge you have, and increase in certainty that it is sent down from God, and in monotheism. The meaning of ﴿Will you then submit?﴾ is: will you be sincere (*mukhlisun*)?

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verse 15:

﴿Whoever desires the life of this world and its adornment – We will pay them in full for their deeds therein, and they will not be deprived therein.﴾ We deliver to them the wages of their deeds complete and whole, without any deprivation, in this world; and this is what they are given therein of health and provision. They are the disbelievers, or the hypocrites.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verse 16:

﴿Those are the ones for whom there is nothing in the Hereafter but the Fire, and what they did therein has come to nothing.﴾ And what they did (ṣanaʿū) or their work (ṣanīʿuhum) came to nothing in the Hereafter, meaning: there was no reward for them, because they did not intend by it the Hereafter; they intended only the worldly life, and what they wanted was paid to them in full. ﴿And what they used to do is worthless.﴾ Meaning: their action was, in itself, worthless, because it was not done for a valid purpose. And knowledge that is worthless has no reward.

﴿Is one who is upon a clear proof (bayyina) from his Lord﴾ [equal to] one who desires the life of this world? So [as for] one who is upon a clear proof from his Lord, that is: they do not follow them in rank, nor do they come near them. This means there is a clear disparity between the two groups. By them is meant those among the Jews who believed, such as ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām and others. "Upon a clear proof from his Lord" means upon a proof (burhān) from God and a clarification that the religion of Islam is true, and this is the proof of reason. ﴿And there follows it﴾, i.e., follows that proof, ﴿a witness﴾ who testifies to its soundness, which is the Qur'an, ﴿from Him﴾, from God, or from the Qur'an, since its mention has already passed. ﴿And before it﴾, before the Qur'an, ﴿was the Book of Moses﴾, which is the Torah. That is: this proof is also followed, before the Qur'an, by the Book of Moses, peace be upon him, ﴿as a guide﴾, a book followed in religion and an exemplar in it, ﴿and a mercy﴾, and a great blessing upon those to whom it was sent down. These two are both ḥāl (circumstantial accusatives). ﴿They believe in it﴾, i.e., those who are upon a clear proof, ﴿they believe in it﴾, in the Qur'an. ﴿But whoever disbelieves in it﴾, in the Qur'an, ﴿among the confederates﴾, meaning the people of Makkah and those who joined them from among those banding together against the Messenger of God (ﷺ), ﴿the Fire is his appointed place﴾, his destination and his place of arrival. ﴿So be not in doubt﴾, in suspicion, ﴿about it﴾, about the Qur'an or about the appointed place, ﴿indeed it is the truth from your Lord, but most people do not believe﴾. (p-52)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verse 18:

﴿Who does greater wrong than one who fabricates a lie against Allah? Those will be presented before their Lord﴾ They will be detained at the place of standing (al-mawqif), and their deeds will be displayed. ﴿And the witnesses will say, "These are the ones who lied against their Lord."﴾ The witnesses (al-ashhad) from among the angels and the prophets will testify against them that they were the liars against Allah, claiming that He took a son and a partner. ﴿Surely, the curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers﴾, meaning those who lied against their Lord. Al-ashhad is the plural of shahid, like ashab and sahib, or of shahid (witness/martyr), like sharif and ashraf.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verse 19:

﴿Those who bar (people) from the way of Allah﴾ — they turn people away from His religion. ﴿and seek to make it crooked﴾ — they describe it as crooked, though it is straight; or they seek to make its adherents become crooked by apostasy. ﴿And they, in the Hereafter, they are disbelievers﴾ — the second "they" (hum) is for emphasis on their disbelief in the Hereafter and to specify them as its (exclusive) possessors.

"Those" (هَؤُلَاءِ/أُولَئِكَ) "have not been" — i.e., they "were not" — ﴿such people⁠—⁠they were not able to escape⁠﴾... 

Let me give the translation properly:

﴿Those⁠—they have not been⁠﴾ meaning: they were not ﴿able to frustrate Allah⁠﴾ on earth, i.e., they could not escape Allah in this world if He wished to punish them. ﴿And they had no protectors besides Allah⁠﴾: no one who would take charge of them, help them against Him, or shield them from His punishment. However, He gave them respite and delayed their punishment until this Day. This is part of the speech of the witnesses. ﴿Their punishment will be doubled⁠﴾, because they led the people astray from the religion of Allah. "Yudda'afu" (is doubled) is read with the doubling of the ʿayn (yuḍaʿʿafu) by Makki and Shami. ﴿They could not bear to hear⁠﴾, i.e., to listen to the truth, ﴿and they used not to see⁠﴾ the truth.

"Those are the ones who have lost themselves" (﴿أُولَئِكَ الَّذِينَ خَسِرُوا أنْفُسَهُمْ﴾), in that they bartered the worship of God for the worship of idols. "And that which they used to invent has departed from them" (﴿وَضَلَّ عَنْهُمْ﴾): it was nullified and lost to them, and what they had purchased is gone, namely "what they used to invent" (﴿ما كانُوا يَفْتَرُونَ﴾) of the deities and their intercession.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verse 22:

﴿Without doubt, they will be the greatest losers in the Hereafter﴾ through their barring (from the path of God) and their turning away. Regarding "lā jaram" there are several opinions. The first: "lā" is a rejection of a preceding statement, meaning: the matter is not as they claimed. The meaning of "jaram" is "kasaba" (he earned/merited), its subject is an implied pronoun, and "annahum fī al-ākhirah" is in the accusative position (maḥall al-naṣb). The estimated sense is: their saying earned them their loss in the Hereafter. The second: "lā jaram" is two words that were compounded, so their meaning became "ḥaqqan" (truly, certainly), and "anna" is in the nominative position, as its subject (fā'il) for "ḥaqqa," meaning: their loss is certain. The third: its meaning is "lā maḥālah" (undoubtedly, without fail).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verse 23:

﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds and humble themselves before their Lord﴾ and feel secure in Him and devote themselves to His worship with humility and lowliness, from "al-khabt," which is low-lying land that is level and firm. ﴿Those are the companions of Paradise; they will abide therein eternally.﴾

The likeness of the two parties is like the blind and the deaf versus the seeing and the hearing. He likened the party of the disbelievers to the blind and the deaf, and the party of the believers to the seeing and the hearing. ﴿Are the two equal in likeness?﴾ meaning the two parties. ﴿Mathalan﴾ (as a likeness): it is in the accusative as a tamyiz (specification). ﴿Will you not then take heed?﴾ so that you benefit from the striking of the parable.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verse 25:

﴿And indeed We sent Noah to his people: "Indeed, I am to you a clear warner."﴾ That is, "that I..." The meaning is: We sent him accompanied by this statement, which is his saying, "Indeed, I am to you a clear warner," (p-54) with a kasra (on the alif of innī). When the preposition became attached to it, it was given a fatha, just as it is given a fatha in "ka'anna" (as if), while the meaning remains that of the kasra. Reading it with a kasra on the alif (innī) is the reading of Ibn Amir (al-Shami), Nafi', ʿAsim and Hamza, understood as implying the act of saying (al-qawl).

"That" (an-) is explanatory (mufassira), connected either to "We sent" or to "a warner." ﴿That you worship none but Allah.﴾ ﴿Indeed I fear for you the punishment of a painful day.﴾ Describing the day as "painful" is a metaphorical attribution (al-isnad al-majazi), since the pain occurs in it.

Then the chiefs among his people who disbelieved said: ﴿So the chiefs who disbelieved among his people said﴾. He means the nobles (al-ashraf), because they fill hearts with awe and their assemblies with dignity, and because they are filled with forbearance and sound opinions. ﴿We see you only as a human being like us﴾. They meant that he should have been an angel (مَلَكًا *malakan*) or a king (مَلِكًا *malikan*). ﴿And we see none following you except those who are our lowest﴾: *akhissa'unā*, the plural of *al-arhal*, meaning our basest. ﴿Bādiya al-ra'y﴾: with a hamza, Abu 'Amr; and without a hamza, Abu 'Amr. That is, they followed you in outward opinion (ẓāhira al-ra'y) or at first opinion (awwala al-ra'y). It is derived from *bada yabdu*, meaning "it appeared," or from *bada'a yabda'u*, meaning "he did a thing first." Its case is that of an adverb of time (ẓarf), and its underlying form is: "at the time of the appearance of their outward opinion or the first of their opinion." That was omitted, and the genitive complement was put in its place. They meant that their following you was something that occurred to them immediately (badīha), without reflection (rawiyya) or consideration. Had they reflected, they would not have followed you. They despised the believers only because of their poverty and their lagging behind in worldly means, because they were ignorant and knew only an outward aspect of the worldly life. Thus the nobles in their eyes were whoever had status and wealth, as you see most of those who imitate Islam believe, and on this they build their honouring and their humiliating of people. They forgot that advancement in this world does not bring anyone closer to God; rather it distances him, and it does not raise him up but lowers him. ﴿And we see no superiority for you over us﴾ in wealth or opinion. They meant Noah and his followers. ﴿Rather we think you are liars﴾: that is, Noah in his call, and his followers in their response and their acceptance. They mean: you colluded in the call and the response, in order to seize leadership (tasbīban li-l-ri'āsa). (p-55)

He said, "O my people, have you considered?" Tell me, "if I am upon a clear proof" (burhan) "from my Lord," and a witness from Him testifies to the truth of my claim, "and He has given me mercy from Himself," meaning prophethood, "but it has been made obscure to you," that is, it has been concealed. Hamza, ʿAlī and Ḥafṣ read it as "uʿammiyat" (passive, with the sense of "it was concealed"). That is, the clear proof has become obscure to you, so it does not guide you, just as when a people's guide becomes blind in a desert wasteland, they remain without a guide. Its real meaning is that the proof, though it was made clear and visible, has been made blind, because the blind person neither finds the way nor guides anyone else. "Shall we compel you to accept it," that is, the mercy, "while you are averse to it?" meaning you do not want it. The wāw (in "wa-antum") has been added here to complete the mīm (in "alzimukumūha"). It is reported from Abū ʿAmr that he read the mīm with a sukūn (in "alzimukum"). Its explanation is that the vowel was only a very slight, fleeting sound, so the narrator took it to be a sukūn, but this is a lahn (a grammatical error), because the inflectional vowel (ḥarakat al-iʿrāb, the vowel marking case) may not be dropped except out of ḍarūrat al-shiʿr (poetic necessity, the license poets are allowed).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verse 29:

﴿And, O my people, I do not ask you for wealth in return for it﴾: that is, for conveying the message, since it is implied by his saying, ﴿Indeed, I am a clear warner to you.﴾ ﴿Wealth﴾: a reward that would weigh heavily on you if you paid it, or on me if you refused. ﴿Indeed, my reward﴾ is read by Madani, Shami, Abu 'Amr and Hafs as ﴿Inna ajri﴾. ﴿My reward is only from Allah. And I will not drive away those who have believed﴾: this is a reply to them when they asked him to drive them away so that they would believe in him, out of disdain at sitting with them. ﴿Indeed, they are going to meet their Lord﴾: so they will complain about me to Him if I drive them away. ﴿But I see you as a people who are ignorant﴾: you act foolishly toward the believers and call them the lowly ones; or, you are ignorant of the meeting with your Lord; or, they are better than you.
﴿O my people, who would help me against God?﴾ That is, who would protect me from His retribution? ﴿If I drive them away, will you not remember?﴾ That is, will you not take heed? (p-56)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verse 31:

﴿And I do not say to you, "With me are the treasuries of Allah"﴾ — so that I would claim a superiority over you in wealth — until you deny my superiority by your saying, "We do not see that you have any merit over us." ﴿Nor do I know the unseen﴾ — until I could know what is within the souls of my followers and the inner thoughts of their hearts. It is conjoined to "With me are the treasuries," meaning: I do not say, "With me are the treasuries of Allah," nor do I say, "I know the unseen." ﴿Nor do I say, "I am an angel"﴾ — until you say to me, "You are only a human being like us." ﴿Nor do I say of those whom your eyes look down upon﴾ — nor do I pass judgment on those among the believers whom you consider lowly because of their poverty. ﴿Allah will not give them any good﴾ — in this world and the Hereafter — because of His contempt for them, in support of you and in accommodation to your desires. ﴿Allah knows best what is within their souls﴾ — of sincerity of belief. It is incumbent upon me only to accept the outward confession, since I do not have access to their hidden secrets. ﴿Indeed, I would then be among the wrongdoers﴾ — if I were to say any such thing. And "al-izdira'" (looking down upon, disdain) is an iftila' form from "zara 'alayhi" when he disparaged him; its origin is "tazta'ri," and the ta' was changed to dal.

﴿They said, "O Noah, you have disputed with us and multiplied your disputing with us, so bring us what you threaten us with, if you are among the truthful."﴾

Disputed with us: contended with us (khasamtana). Multiplied our disputing: you made our argument great (fa-aktharta jidalana). Bring us what you promise us: of the punishment (min al-adhab). If you are among the truthful: in your promise (fi wa'dika).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verse 33:

﴿He said: "Only Allah will bring it upon you, if He wills."﴾ That is: the bringing of the punishment is not up to me; it is up to Him, the One you have disbelieved in. ﴿And you cannot escape.﴾ That is: you will not be able to flee from it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 11, verse 34:

﴿And my advice will not benefit you﴾ means informing you of the place of error (*ghayy*) so that it may be avoided, and of right guidance (*rushd*) so that it may be followed. The words "لَكِنِّيَ"، "إنِّيَ"، "نُصْحِيَ" are read with a final *ya'* by al-Madani and Abu 'Amr. ﴿If I wish to advise you, if Allah wishes to lead you astray﴾, i.e., to send you astray. This is a conditional clause entering upon another conditional clause, so the second is placed first in meaning, as is known. Its sense is: "If Allah wishes to lead you astray, my advice will not benefit you, if I wish to advise you." This is a clear proof for us regarding the will of Allah concerning acts of disobedience. ﴿He is your Lord﴾, so He disposes of you according to His will, ﴿and to Him you will be returned﴾, so He will recompense you for your deeds.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verse 35:

﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"?﴾ Rather, do they say, "He has invented it"? ﴿Say: If I have invented it, then upon me is the punishment of my crime﴾, i.e., if it is established that I have invented it, then upon me is the punishment of my crime, that is, my inventing it. It is said: "ajrama al-rajul" (he committed a crime) when he sinned. ﴿And I am innocent﴾, i.e., and it is not established that this is so, and I am innocent of it. As for ﴿of what you commit as crimes﴾, it means of your crime in attributing the fabrication to me, so there is no justification for your turning away and your hostility.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verse 36:

﴿And it was revealed to Noah: "None of your people will believe except those who have already believed."﴾ This is a despairing of their faith, and that it is not to be expected. In it is evidence that faith is subject to renewal (tajaddud), as if he had said: "Whoever has believed, believes at the time of the occurrence." On this basis the increase in faith mentioned in connection with the Qur'an is to be explained. ﴿So do not grieve over what they used to do.﴾ That is, do not grieve with the grief of one who is wretched and humbled. The verb ibti’as (ibti'as) is a form of the verbal pattern ifti'al derived from ba's (bu's), which means grief or poverty. The meaning is: do not grieve over what they did of denying you and harming you, for the time of retribution against your enemies has come.

﴿And make the ship under Our eyes﴾. This is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl, the grammatical term for a circumstantial accusative), meaning: make it while it is protected. Its real sense is: while it is in Our eyes, as though God has eyes that watch over him, lest he deviate from what is correct in his craftsmanship. ﴿And by Our inspiration﴾, for We reveal to you and inspire you in how you should make it. On the authority of Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both: he did not know how the ship was to be built, so Allah revealed to him that he should make it like the breast (juʾjuʾ) of a bird. ﴿And do not address Me concerning those who have done wrong﴾, meaning do not call upon Me regarding your people, seeking to repel the punishment from them through your intercession. ﴿Indeed they are to be drowned﴾, meaning they are decreed to be drowned. It has already been determined and the pen has dried, so there is no way to avert it.

(p. 58)

[Qur'an 11:38] "And he was making the ark." This describes a past situation.

"And whenever a group of the chiefs of his people passed by him, they mocked him." They mocked him for his making of the ship, and he was building it in a desert, in the place furthest from water. So they laughed at him and said to him: "O Nuh, you have become a carpenter after you were a prophet."

"He said: If you mock us, then we shall mock you" at the sight of destruction, "just as you mock us" at the sight of the ark.

It is narrated that Nuh, peace be upon him, made the ship from teak wood in two years. Its length was three hundred cubits, or one thousand two hundred cubits, and its breadth was fifty cubits, or six hundred cubits, and its height in the sky was thirty cubits. He made it with three decks. In the lowest deck he carried the wild animals, the predators and the creeping things; in the middle deck the beasts and livestock; and Nuh and those with him rode in the highest deck, together with what they needed of provisions. He also carried with him the body of Adam, peace be upon him, and made it a barrier between men and women.

Qur'an 11:39: "So you will know who it is that will receive a punishment that disgraces him, and upon whom will descend a lasting punishment."

Al-Nasafi, Madarik al-Tanzil: "﴿So you will know﴾ ﴿who it is that will come to him﴾ — 'man' is in the accusative position as the object of 'ta'lamun' (you will know), meaning: so you will know the one who will come to him ﴿a punishment that will disgrace him﴾. By 'him' is meant them (the people), and by 'punishment' is meant the punishment of this world, which is drowning. ﴿And there will descend upon him﴾ — i.e., will alight upon him ﴿a lasting punishment﴾, which is the punishment of the Hereafter."

(p-59) "Ḥattā" (until) is the particle after which a sentence begins. It is attached to a sentence made of a conditional clause and its consequent, and it marks the endpoint (ghāyah) of his words "and he was making the ark." That is, he kept making it until the time of the appointed promise came. The discourse between them is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) qualifying "yaṣnaʿu" (he was making). That is, he was making it while, whenever a group of the chiefs of his people passed by him, they mocked him. The answer to "kullamā" (whenever) is "sakhirū" (they mocked), and "qāla" (he said) is either a resumptive sentence, as if answering a questioner's question, or "qāla" is the answer. "Sakhirū" is either a substitute (badal) for "marra" or a qualifier (ṣifah) for "malaʾ" (chiefs). ﴿When Our command came﴾, meaning Our punishment, ﴿and the oven gushed forth﴾. This is a metaphor (kināyah) for the intensification and severity of the matter. It is also said that its meaning is that water welled up from the baking oven, and it was made of stone belonging to Ḥawwāʾ (Eve), and it came into the possession of Nūḥ (peace be upon him). It is also said that "al-tannūr" means the surface of the earth. ﴿We said: Load into it﴾, into the ship, ﴿from every kind two of each pair﴾. Its explanation is in Surat al-Muʾminūn. ﴿And your family, except those against whom the word has already preceded﴾ is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to "ithnayn" (two). Likewise ﴿and those who believe﴾, meaning: load your family and the believers from among others. He excepted from his family those against whom the word had preceded, that he is among the people of the Fire. The word had preceded against him only because of Allah's knowledge that he would choose disbelief by His decree and will, exalted is the Creator of the servants above anything in existence contrary to what He willed. ﴿And none believed with him except a few.﴾ The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "They were eight: Nūḥ, his family, his three sons, and their wives." It is also said that they were ten: five men and five women. It is also said that they were seventy-two men and women. The sons of Nūḥ were Sām, Ḥām and Yāfith, and their wives; so the total is seventy-eight, half of them men and half of them women.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verse 41:

﴿And he said, "Embark upon it; in the name of Allah is its course and its anchorage."﴾ "Bismillah" (in the name of Allah) is connected to "irkabū" (embark) as a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative, a phrase describing the state of the subject) from the wāw (the plural subject pronoun in "irkabū"). That is: "Embark upon it while naming Allah," or "saying 'in the name of Allah' at the time of its sailing and at the time of its anchoring." This is either because the "majrā" (course) and the "mursā" (anchorage) are for a time (ẓarf, adverb of time), or because they are both maṣdars (verbal nouns) like "ijrā'" (sailing) and "irsā'" (anchoring), from which the time-noun is omitted, being a muḍāf (a noun in a construct phrase whose second term is elided), as in their saying "khufūqa al-najm" (the twinkling of the star).

It is also permissible for "Bismillah majrāhā wa mursāhā" to be an independent sentence, not connected to what precedes it, consisting of a mubtada' (subject) and khabar (predicate). The meaning is that Noah (peace be upon him) commanded them to board, then informed them that its course and its anchorage are by the mention of Allah's name, i.e., "In the name of Allah is its sailing and its anchoring." And whenever he wished it to sail, he would say "Bismillah," and it sailed; and whenever he wished it to anchor, he would say "Bismillah," and it anchored.

"Majrīhā" (with a fatḥah on the mīm and a kasrah on the rā', from jarā) is read as either a maṣdar or a time-noun by Ḥamzah, ʿAlī and Ḥafṣ. Abū ʿAmr reads it with a ḍammah on the mīm and a kasrah on the rā', and the rest read it with a ḍammah on the mīm and a fatḥah on the rā'. [p-60]

﴿Indeed, my Lord is Most Forgiving﴾ toward whoever among them believed, ﴿Most Merciful﴾ in that He delivered them.

﴿And it sails with them﴾ is connected (*muttasil*, grammatically linked) to an omitted element implied by "ارْكَبُوا فِيها بِسْمِ اللهِ" ("Embark therein, in the name of God"). It is as if it were said: "So they embarked therein, saying, 'In the name of God,' and it sails with them," meaning: the ship sails while they are in it. ﴿Amid waves like mountains﴾ means the waves of the Flood. "Mawj" is the plural of "mawjah," as "tamr" is the plural of "tamrah" (a collective noun and its singular). It is the water that rises when it is agitated by the force of violent winds entering it. Each wave of it is compared to a mountain in its massing and height.

﴿And Noah called out to his son﴾: Kan'an, and it was said Yam. The majority hold that he was his biological son, but it was also said that he was the son of his wife [from another marriage]. ﴿And he was in an isolated place﴾ away from his father and away from the ship. "Ma'zil" is a noun of place on the pattern "maf'il," from "‘azalahu ‘anhu," meaning when one pushes him away and removes him. Or it means he was in an isolated place away from his father's religion.

﴿O my son﴾: ‘Asim read it with a fatha on the ya' (*yā bunayya*), treating it as a truncation (*iqtisar*) of the alif that replaces the ya' of possession, from your saying "yā bunayyā." Others read it with a kasra on the ya' as a truncation of the ya' of possession. ﴿Embark with us﴾ on the ship; that is: submit and embark. ﴿And do not be with the disbelievers.﴾

﴿He said, "I will take refuge"﴾ *ألْجَأُ* (I will seek shelter) ﴿"on a mountain that will protect me from the water."﴾ *يَعْصِمُنِي مِنَ الماءِ* (it will prevent me from the water), *يَمْنَعُنِي مِنَ الغَرَقِ* (it will keep me from drowning). ﴿He said, "Today there is no protector from the command of God, except for the one on whom He has mercy."﴾ That is, except the One who has mercy, who is God, the Exalted; or it means: today there is no protector from the flood except the one on whom God has mercy, i.e., except in the place of those among the believers on whom God has had mercy. This is because when he [Noah] made the mountain a protector from the water, [God] said to him: "No one who seeks refuge in a mountain or the like will be protected by it today, except for one place of refuge: the place of those whom God has had mercy on and saved," meaning the ship. Or it is an *istithna' munqati'* (disjunctive exception), as if it were said: "But the one on whom God has mercy is the one who is protected," like His saying ﴿They have no knowledge of it, except the following of assumption﴾ [al-Nisa': 157]. ﴿And the wave came between them﴾ between his son and the mountain, or between Noah and his son (p-٦١) ﴿so he was among the drowned﴾, i.e., he became [one of them], or it means he was [so] in the knowledge of God.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on Surah 11, verse 44:**

﴿And it was said: "O earth, swallow your water,"﴾ meaning: soak it up and drink it in. *Al-bal'* (swallowing) is *al-nashf* (soaking up). ﴿"And O sky, withhold"﴾ meaning: hold back. ﴿And the water subsided﴾ meaning: it decreased. It comes from *ghādahu*, when one says *ghāḍahu* ("he diminished it"), and the verb is both intransitive and transitive. ﴿And the command was fulfilled﴾ meaning: He carried out what Allah had promised Noah regarding the destruction of his people. ﴿And it settled﴾ meaning: the ship came to rest, *istaqarrat*, after it had drifted over the whole earth for six months. ﴿On al-Judi﴾, which is a mountain in Mosul. ﴿And it was said: "Away with the wrongdoing people!"﴾ meaning: destruction to the people of Noah who were drowned. It is said *ba'uda ba'dan wa ba'adan* when they wish for the deepest remoteness, namely from the place of destruction and death. For this reason it is specified as a curse of evil.

The examination of this verse proceeds from four aspects.

**First, from the standpoint of ʿilm al-bayān** (the science of eloquent expression), which is the examination of the figurative language (*majāz*), metaphor (*istiʿāra*) and metonymy (*kināya*) it contains and what is connected with them. We say that when Allah, exalted is He, wished to express the meaning of: "We willed to return what gushed forth from the earth into its belly, so it returned; and to cut off the flood of the sky, so it was cut off; and to make the water that descended from the sky subside, so it subsided; and to decree the matter of Noah, which is the fulfilment of what We had promised him concerning the drowning of his people, so it was decreed; and to make the ship settle on al-Judi, so it settled; and We left the wrongdoers drowned," the speech was built upon likening the willed thing to the commanded one, which cannot disobey because of the perfection of its awe, and likening the bringing-into-being of the willed thing to the decisive command that takes effect in the coming-to-be of the intended thing. This was a depiction of His great power, and that the heavens and the earth are subservient to His bringing into being within them whatever He wills, without being able to resist His will to change and alter them, as though they were discerning intelligent beings who knew Him as He truly should be known, understood with certainty the obligation to submit to His command and to yield to His judgment, and the necessity of exerting maximum effort to achieve His will. Then, upon this likeness, he arranged the structure of the speech, saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿"And it was said"﴾ by way of metaphor for the will, which occurs through its cause, the saying of the speaker. He made the indicator of the metaphor the address to inanimate things, which is ﴿"O earth"﴾ and ﴿"O sky"﴾. Then he said, addressing them: "O earth, and O sky," by way of metaphor (p. 62) for the stated likeness. Then he used as a metaphor, for the sinking of water into the earth, the *bal'* (swallowing), which is the action of drawing in food, because of the resemblance between them, namely going to a hidden resting place. Then he used "water" as a metaphor for nourishment, likening it to food, since the earth is strengthened by water in producing vegetation just as the eater is strengthened by food. Then he said ﴿"your water"﴾, attributing the water to the earth by way of metaphor, because the water is connected to the earth as ownership is connected to the owner. Then he chose for the withholding of the rain the *iqlāʿ* (ceasing), which is the agent's abandoning of an action, because of the resemblance between them in the lack of deliberation. Then he said ﴿"And the water subsided, and the command was fulfilled, and it settled on al-Judi. And it was said: 'Away with them!'"﴾, and he did not state who caused the water to subside, nor who decreed the matter, nor who levelled the ship, nor who said "Away." He likewise did not state who said "O earth" and "O sky," pursuing in each of these the path of metonymy, and indicating that such great matters cannot occur except through the act of a capable agent and the bringing-into-being of an overpowering creator, and that their doer is one who has no partner in his act. So the mind does not conceive that anyone else might say "O earth, swallow your water, and O sky, withhold," nor that anyone other than Him causes the subsiding, decreeing and levelling. Then he concluded the speech with an indirect allusion, as a warning to those who followed the path of denying the messengers, wronging themselves, in order to show the place of wrath, and that this severe punishment was only because of their wrongdoing.

**Second, from the standpoint of ʿilm al-maʿānī** (the science of meanings), which is the examination of the function of each word in it and the purpose of each instance of advancing or delaying among its clauses. The word ﴿"O" (yā)﴾ was chosen over its sister particles because it is the most commonly used, and because it indicates the distance of the one addressed, which the situation requires in order to display greatness and sovereignty and to show might and dominion. It is the distancing of the one addressed, which signals a lack of concern for him. He did not say *yā arḍī* ("O my earth") because a possessive suffix increases the sense of disregard, since the pronominal attachment requires nearness. He did not say *yā ayyatuhā al-arḍ* ("O earth") for the sake of brevity. The words "earth" and "sky" were chosen because they are lighter and more frequent. ﴿"Swallow" (ibla'ī)﴾ was chosen over *ibtali'ī* because it is more concise, and for the sake of assonance between it and *aqli'ī* ("withhold"). It is said that *aqli'ī* was used without specifying "from the rain." Likewise he did not say "O earth, swallow your water," so it swallowed, "and O sky, withhold," so it withheld, for brevity. Or it was chosen as *ghīḍa* instead of *ghuyyida*. It is said "the water" without saying "the water of the flood." And "the command," without saying "the command of Noah and his people," for the purpose of brevity and of relying on the definite article to indicate that reference. He did not say *wa-suwwiyat ʿalā al-Judi* ("and it was levelled upon al-Judi"), meaning it remained in the manner of *qīla* and *ghīḍa*, out of regard for the construction of the verb with an active subject, together with the ship in His words ﴿"and it sailed with them"﴾ (11:42), intending agreement. Then ﴿"Away with the people"﴾ was said, and he did not say *li-yabʿad al-qawm* ("let the people be removed"), seeking emphasis together with brevity. This is the examination from the viewpoint of the composition of the words. As for the examination from the viewpoint of the arrangement of the clauses, he placed the address before the command, saying ﴿"O earth, swallow, and O sky, withhold"﴾, and he did not say *ibla'ī yā arḍu wa-aqli'ī yā samāʾu*, following the requirement of speech addressed to one who is truly commanded, by placing the alert first so that the command that follows it may be firmly established in the mind of the one addressed, intending thereby the sense of *tarshīḥ* (reinforcement). Then he put the earth before the command to the sky and began with it, because the flood began from it. Then he followed with ﴿"the water subsided"﴾ because it is connected with the story of the water and its seizing of them by the waist. Then he mentioned what was the real purpose, which is his saying ﴿"and the command was fulfilled"﴾, meaning: He fulfilled the promise of destroying the disbelievers and saving Noah and those with him in the ark. Based on this, reflect.

**Third, from the standpoint of semantic eloquence** (*faṣāḥa maʿnawiyya*), which is, as you see, a delicate arrangement of meanings and a rendering of them that is condensed and clear, with no complexity that trips up thought in seeking the intended meaning, and no crookedness that makes the path to the seeker unclear.

**Fourth, from the standpoint of verbal eloquence** (*faṣāḥa lafẓiyya*). Its words, as you see, are Arabic, in common use, sound, free from discordance, far from harshness, sweet upon the palate, smooth upon the tongue. Each of them is like water in smoothness, like honey in sweetness, and like the breeze in gentleness. For this reason the opponents have unanimously agreed that human capacity falls short of producing the like of this verse. By Allah, how excellent is the character of the revelation! The scholar does not contemplate any of its verses without perceiving subtleties that cannot be contained by enumeration. Do not suppose that the verse is limited to what has been mentioned, for perhaps what has been left out is more than what has been written down.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 11, verse 45:

﴿And Noah called out to his Lord and said, "My Lord"﴾. His calling out to his Lord is his supplication to Him, and it is his saying "My Lord," together with what follows it, which demands the fulfillment of His promise to deliver his family. ﴿Indeed, my son is of my family﴾, meaning: some of my family, because he was his son from his own loins, or he was a stepson (*rabib*) to him, and so he was part of his family. ﴿And indeed, Your promise is true﴾: every promise You make is the true, established promise, about whose fulfillment and carrying out there is no doubt, and You have promised me that You would deliver my family, so what is the matter with my son? ﴿And You are the most just of judges (al-hakimin)﴾, meaning: the most knowledgeable of judges and the most just of them, since a judge has no superiority over another except through knowledge and justice. Many a person drowned in ignorance and injustice among those entrusted with judgeship in your time has been given the title *qadi al-qudat* (chief judge), whose meaning is "the most judicious of judges." So take heed and learn a lesson. (p-64)

He said: "O Noah, he is not of your family." Then he gave the reason that he is not of his family in His saying: ﴿Indeed, he is one whose conduct is not righteous﴾. In this there is an indication that kinship in religion overrides kinship by blood, and that your relative in religion, even if he is an Abyssinian while you are a Qurashi, is your closest kin, whereas one who is not upon your religion, even if he is the nearest of your relatives by blood, is the most distant of the distant from you. His very being was made into "conduct that is not righteous" as an intensification of his blame, like the saying of the poetess:

"...... *** for it is only advance and retreat."

Or the estimate is: "Indeed, he is one who has (bad) conduct." And there is in it an indication that he only saved those of his family who were saved because of their righteousness, not because they were his family. When righteousness was absent from him, his fatherhood did not benefit him.

"ʿAmila ghayra ṣāliḥ" (ʿAlī's reading). Abū Manṣūr, may God have mercy on him, said: Noah, peace be upon him, had thought that his son was upon his religion, because he was a hypocrite. Otherwise it is not conceivable that he would say "my son is of my family" and ask Him to save him, when He had already forbidden him from asking the like of that, saying: ﴿And do not address Me concerning those who have wronged; indeed, they are to be drowned﴾ [Hud: 37]. So he asked Him according to the outward appearance that he had, just as the hypocrites used to show agreement with our Prophet (ﷺ) while concealing opposition to him. He did not know of this until God informed him of it. His saying ﴿he is not of your family﴾ means: not of those whom I promised salvation, who are the believers in truth, inwardly and outwardly.

"Fa-lā tasʾalnī" with the vowel-kasra standing in for the yā' is the Kūfī reading; "tasʾalnī" is the Baṣrī reading; "tasʾalnīya" is the Madanī reading; "tasʾalnn" is the Shāmī reading, where the yā' is dropped and the kasra stands in for it, and the nūn is the nūn of emphasis; "tasʾalanna" is the Makkī reading. ﴿about which you have no knowledge﴾, namely, the permissibility of asking Him for it. ﴿I admonish you lest you be among the ignorant﴾: this is like what He forbade our Prophet (ﷺ) with His saying: ﴿So do not be among the ignorant﴾ [al-Anʿām: 35].

﴿He said, "My Lord, I seek refuge in You from asking You for that of which I have no knowledge."﴾ That is: from asking You in the future for anything whose correctness I have no knowledge of, showing good manners in following Your manners and taking warning from Your admonition. ﴿And unless You forgive me﴾ for what has passed from me ﴿and have mercy on me﴾ by ʿiṣmah (divine preservation from sin) against returning to the like of it, ﴿I will be among the losers.﴾

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verse 48:

﴿It was said: "O Noah, descend with peace from Us"﴾, meaning with a greeting from Us, or with safety from the drowning. ﴿And blessings upon you﴾: these are the growing goods, and for him they are in the abundance of his offspring and followers. For most of the prophets were made from his descendants, and the leaders of the religion in the later centuries are from his lineage. ﴿And upon nations from those with you﴾: the word ﴿مِن﴾ (min) here is for explanation (li-l-bayan), so the nations meant are those who were with him in the ship, since they were groups, or it was said that they were called nations because nations branch out from them. Or the ﴿مِن﴾ is for the beginning of the extent (li-ibtida' al-ghayah), meaning: upon nations arising from those with you, and these are the nations until the end of time. This is the more likely view. ﴿And nations﴾ is in the nominative case as the subject (mubtada'). ﴿We will provide for them﴾ in this world with abundance of provision and ease of living. This clause is a description (sifah), and the predicate (khabar) is omitted; its estimated form is: "And from those with you are nations We will provide for them." It was omitted because ﴿مِمَّنْ مَعَكَ﴾ (from those with you) indicates it. ﴿Then a painful punishment from Us will touch them﴾: that is, in the Hereafter. The meaning is that peace from Us and blessings upon you and upon believing nations who will arise from those with you, and from those with you are nations given enjoyment in this world who will be turned back to the Fire. Noah, peace be upon him, was the father of the prophets, and all creation after the Flood descended from him and from those who were with him in the ship. It is also reported from Muhammad ibn Ka'b that this peace includes every believing man and woman until the Day of Resurrection, and that the enjoyment and punishment that follow it include every disbeliever.

(p-66) ﴿That﴾ is a demonstrative referring to the story of Noah, peace be upon him. Its position is nominative (marfu') as the subject, al-ibtida' (inchoative), and the sentences after it, which are ﴿among the tidings of the unseen, We reveal them to you; neither you nor your people knew them before this﴾, are predicates, akhbar. That is, this story is part of the tidings of the unseen, revealed to you, unknown to you and to your people, ﴿before this﴾ time, or before My revelation to you and your being informed of it. ﴿So be patient﴾ in conveying the message and in bearing the harm of your people, as Noah was patient, and expect for yourself and for those who denied you the same kind of outcome that Noah and his people had. ﴿Indeed, the final outcome﴾ in success, victory and triumph ﴿is for the God-fearing﴾, those who guard themselves against polytheism.

And to ʿĀd [We sent] their brother Hūd, (a single man from among them); its being in the accusative is by coordination with "We sent Noah," meaning: and We sent to ʿĀd their brother ﴿Hūd﴾, which is an explicative apposition (ʿaṭf bayān). ﴿He said: O my people, worship Allah﴾, make Him one (waḥḥidūhu). ﴿You have no god other than Him﴾. With the nominative (rafʿ), Nāfiʿ reads it, as an attribute (ṣifa) of the place of the preposition and its object (maḥall al-jārr wa-l-majrūr); and with the genitive (jarr), ʿAlī reads it, in accordance with the wording (lafẓ). ﴿You are only fabricators﴾, you invent against Allah the lie by taking idols as partners to Him.

O my people, I do not ask you for any wealth in return for it; my reward is only from the One who created me (Hud 11:51).

No messenger has ever addressed his people with this statement, because the nature of their mission is sincere advice (nasihah), and sincere advice is not purified except by cutting off all greed. As long as any suspicion of worldly gain remains, the advice will not succeed and will not benefit. ﴿Will you not then use your reason?﴾ For you reject the advice of one who asks no reward for it except from God, which is the reward of the Hereafter, and nothing clears away accusation more than that.

﴿And O my people, ask your Lord for forgiveness﴾ (meaning: believe in Him), ﴿then turn to Him in repentance﴾ (meaning: from worshipping other than Him). ﴿He will send the sky upon you in abundant rain﴾ (meaning: the rain), ﴿مِدْرارًا﴾ (midrāran) is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: ﴿abundant in its pouring﴾. ﴿And He will add strength to your strength﴾. He only intended to win them over to faith by promising abundant rain and increased strength (p-67), because they were people of crops and gardens, and so they were most in need of water. They were also proud of what they had been given of might and power. It is said that he meant strength in wealth, or strength in sexual potency. It is also said that rain had been withheld from them for three years and the wombs of their women had become barren, so Hud, upon him be peace, promised them rain and children in return for faith and seeking forgiveness.

It is related from al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with them both, that a man who was wealthy but had no children came to Muʿāwiya as a delegation. When he left, one of Muʿāwiya's chamberlains said to him: "I am a man of wealth, and I have no children. Teach me something, perhaps Allah will grant me a child." Al-Ḥasan said: "Hold fast to seeking forgiveness." So the man began to seek forgiveness abundantly, to the extent that he would sometimes seek forgiveness seven hundred times in a single day, and he was blessed with ten sons. This reached Muʿāwiya, who said: "Why did you not ask him the reason for saying that?" So on another delegation, the man asked him, and he said: "Have you not heard the words of Hud: ﴿And He will add strength to your strength﴾, and the words of Nuh, upon him be peace: ﴿And He will provide you with wealth and sons﴾ [Nūḥ: 12]?"

﴿And do not turn away﴾, meaning: do not turn away from Me and from what I call you to, ﴿as criminals﴾, meaning: persisting in your crimes and sins.

"They said, 'O Hud, you have not brought us any clear proof'" — a lie and denial on their part, just as the Quraysh said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), 402 like His saying: "And Allah is Knowing of what you do" [29:... ] and "Why was not a sign sent down upon him from his Lord?" [13:7] — with the absence of His signs being limited.

"And we will not leave our gods on account of your word" — this is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "leaving our gods," as if it were said: "And we would not leave our gods, departing from your word."

"And we are not going to believe you" — and it is not valid for the likes of us to believe one like you in what he calls us to, (this is) in despair of him attaining a response.

﴿In naqulu illa i'taraka ba'du alihatina bi-su'in﴾ (We say nothing except that some of our gods have struck you with evil). "In" is a particle of negation, so it negates all speech except one statement, namely their saying "i'taraka" (has struck you): some of our gods have afflicted you with evil, with madness and derangement. Its implied sense is: "We say nothing, except this statement," that is, our saying: "Some of our gods have struck you with evil." ﴿He said: Indeed I call Allah to witness, and bear witness yourselves that I am free from what you associate [with Him]﴾.

(from Commentary of al-Nasafi, Madarik al-Tanzil, on surah 11, verse 55)

﴿Besides Him﴾: that is, besides your associating other gods with Him. The meaning is: "I call God to witness that I am free of what you associate with Him. And you too, bear witness that I am free of that." This is expressed in the form of a command to bear witness, as a man says to one whose moisture has dried up (i.e., one who is withered and useless) between him and himself: "Bear witness that I do not love you," mocking him and belittling his condition. ﴿So scheme against me, all of you﴾, you and your gods, ﴿then give me no respite﴾: do not grant me a delay. For I do not care about you or your scheming, and I do not fear your harm, even if you unite against me. How could your gods harm me, when they are but lifeless matter that neither harms nor benefits? And how could they take revenge on me if I have attacked them and turned away from worshipping them, by afflicting me with madness and taking away my reason?

I have trusted in God, my Lord and your Lord. There is no creature that He does not hold by its forelock. (That is, its owner.) When he mentioned his trust in God and his confidence in His preservation and protection from their plotting, he described Him with what makes trust in Him necessary: that His lordship encompasses him and them, and that every creature is in His grip, under His possession, and under His subjugation and dominion. Seizing by the forelock is an image (tamthil) of this. ﴿Indeed my Lord is on a straight path.﴾ That is: indeed my Lord is upon the truth, from which He never deviates; or, indeed my Lord guides to a straight path.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verse 57:

﴿Then if you turn away, I have already conveyed to you what I was sent with to you.﴾ It is in the position of: the proof has already been established against you. ﴿And my Lord will bring a people other than you in your place.﴾ This is a resumed statement, meaning: Allah will destroy you and bring other people who will succeed you in your dwellings and your wealth. ﴿And you will not harm Him in the least﴾ by your turning away, ﴿anything﴾ of harm at all, since harms are not applicable to Him; rather, you only harm yourselves. ﴿Indeed my Lord is over all things a Guardian (ḥafīẓ)﴾: a watcher over them, a overseer (muhayman) of them, so your deeds are not hidden from Him and He does not neglect to call you to account; or [it means]: One who is a watcher over all things, preserving them, and since things are in need of His preservation from harms, He would not harm the like of him with the like of you.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verse 58:

﴿When Our command came, We saved Hud and those who believed with him﴾ and they were four thousand, ﴿by a mercy from Us﴾, i.e., by a bounty from Us, not by their deeds, or by the faith with which We had favoured them. ﴿And We saved them from a severe punishment﴾. The repetition of "We saved" (najjaynā) is for emphasis, or the second refers to the punishment of the Hereafter, and there is no punishment more severe than it. (p-69)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verse 59:

﴿And that was ʿĀd⦆ — a reference to their graves and their remains, as if he had said: "Travel through the earth, look upon them, and take heed." Then he resumed describing their circumstances, saying: ﴿They denied the signs of their Lord and disobeyed His messengers﴾, because whoever disobeys his messenger has disobeyed all the messengers of Allah. ﴿We make no distinction between any of His messengers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 285].

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verse 60:

﴿And they followed the command of every obstinate tyrant.﴾ [Hud: 59] He means their leaders and their callers to the denial of the Messengers, because they are the ones who compel the people to the affairs and oppose their Lord. The meaning of following their command is obeying them. ﴿And they were followed, in this world, by a curse, and on the Day of Resurrection.﴾ Since they were followers of these leaders rather than of the Messengers, the curse was made to follow them in both abodes. ﴿Verily, ʿAd disbelieved in their Lord. Ala, bu'dan li-ʿAd!﴾ The repetition of "ala" with the vocative, on account of their disbelief and the invocation against them, is to magnify their affair and to urge reflection upon them and caution against the likes of their condition. The invocation "bu'dan" (far away) after their destruction, which is an invocation for destruction, is to indicate that they were deserving of it. ﴿The people of Hud﴾ is an explanatory apposition (ʿatf bayan) to ʿAd, and there is a benefit in it, because ʿAd were of two kinds: the first, the ancient one, which is the people of Hud, and the story concerns them; and the other, Iram.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verse 61:

﴿And to Thamud [We sent] their brother Salih. He said: "O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. He produced you from the earth."﴾ No one produced you from it except Him. Their creation from it is the creation of Adam from dust, then their creation from Adam. ﴿And He settled you in it﴾, and made you its inhabitants (ʿummār, plural of ʿāmir) and desired from you its cultivation (ʿimāra). Or [the verb] istaʿmarakum comes from al-ʿumr (life span), meaning He lengthened your lives in it. Their lifespans ranged from three hundred to a thousand years. The kings of Persia (Fāris) had greatly excavated rivers and planted trees, and they were given long lifespans, along with the injustice that was among them. A prophet of their time asked his Lord about the reason for their long lives, and Allah revealed to him that "they cultivated My lands, so My servants lived in them." ﴿So seek His forgiveness﴾, i.e., ask Him for His forgiveness through faith. ﴿Then turn to Him in repentance; indeed my Lord is near﴾, near in mercy, ﴿responsive﴾ to whoever calls upon Him. (p-70)

They said, "O Salih, you were among us someone we hoped great things from before this," meaning among ourselves, looked to for leadership and for consultation in affairs. Or it means "we used to hope that you would enter our religion and agree with us in what we are upon." "Do you forbid us to worship what our fathers worshipped?" This is a narration of a past state. "And indeed we are in disquieting doubt about what you call us to," namely the affirmation of God's oneness (tawhid), "disquieting" meaning one that brings about doubt (rayb). It is from arabahu, when he caused him to fall into doubt, and doubt is the unrest of the soul and the absence of tranquility.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verse 63:

﴿He said: "O my people, tell me, if I am upon clear evidence from my Lord and He has given me mercy from Himself"﴾ meaning prophethood. He used the particle of doubt (in) although he was certain that he was upon clear evidence, because his address was to the deniers. It is as if he said: "Suppose that I am upon clear evidence from my Lord, and that I am truly a prophet, and consider: if I follow you and disobey my Lord in His commands"﴿then who will help me against Allah﴾ meaning, who will protect me from the punishment of Allah ﴿if I disobey Him﴾ in conveying His message and in preventing you from worshipping idols, ﴿then you would add nothing to me﴾ by your saying: "Does he forbid us to worship what our fathers worshipped?" ﴿but loss﴾ by your attributing to me a loss (khasar), or by my attributing to you a ruin (khusran).

"O my people, this is God's she-camel, a sign for you." [Accusative, as a circumstantial state (ḥāl). The verb-meaning implied by the demonstrative noun (ism al-ishārah, "this") governs it, and "for you" (lakum) is attached to "a sign" (āyah) as a preposed circumstantial qualifier of it. Had it been postponed, it would have been a qualifier (ṣifah) of the noun; since it was placed first, it takes the accusative as a state.] "So leave her to eat on God's earth": i.e., her provision is not incumbent upon you, although her benefit is for you. "And do not touch her with harm": by hamstringing (ʿaqr) or slaughtering (naḥr). "Lest there seize you a near punishment": a swift one.

"﴿So they hamstrung her﴾ on Wednesday. ﴿Then he said﴾ (Salih): ﴿Enjoy yourselves﴾ (istamti'u): take your fill of living ﴿in your homes﴾ (dar), in your land; the lands are called diyar because one manages affairs in them (yudaru fiha, i.e. one acts or disposes), or it means the abode of the world, ﴿for three days﴾, then you will perish. So they perished on Saturday. (p-71) ﴿That is a promise not to be denied﴾: i.e., not denied in it, so the adverbial noun was extended by omitting the preposition and treating it as a direct object; or it means a promise that is not a lie, taking "maktub" as a verbal noun like "ma'qul.""

﴿So when Our command came﴾ [Hud: 82], with the punishment, or Our punishment, ﴿We saved Salih and those who believed with him by a mercy from Us﴾. The Shaykh, may God have mercy on him, said: This indicates that whoever is saved is saved only by the mercy of God Most High, not by his deeds, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "None of you will enter Paradise except by the mercy of God."

﴿And from the disgrace of that day﴾. The word "disgrace" is attached to "day," and "day" is in the genitive by the idafa (construct), and read with a fatha, which is the reading of Madani and ʿAli, because it is attached to idh, which is mabni (indeclinable, fixed in form). When adverbs of time are attached to ambiguous nouns or to past verbs, they become mabni and take their indeclinability from the noun they are attached to, as in the poet's line:

"When I rebuked grey hair over my youth"

The waw is for conjunction, and its implied construction is: "and We saved them from the disgrace of that day," meaning from its humiliation and shame. There is no greater disgrace than the disgrace of one whose destruction came through the anger and vengeance of God. It is also permissible that by "that day" is meant the Day of Resurrection, just as the "severe punishment" has been explained as the punishment of the Hereafter.

﴿Indeed your Lord is the Strong﴾, the one able to save His friends, ﴿the Mighty﴾, the Victorious who destroys His enemies.
﴿And the cry seized those who did wrong﴾, i.e., the cry of Jibril, peace be upon him. ﴿So they became in their homes﴾, their dwellings, ﴿prostrate﴾, dead. (p-72)

﴿As if they had never lived in it﴾, meaning: they did not dwell in it. "Surely Thamud disbelieved in their Lord." The reading "Thamud" (ثَمُودَ) is that of Hamzah and Hafs, without tanwin. ﴿Surely, away with Thamud!﴾ is read as "لِثَمُودٍ" (for Thamudin, with tanwin). The first reading, with ṣarf (declension, i.e. taking tanwin), is for the sense of the tribe or the eponymous forefather. Its non-declension (man') is due to definiteness (ta'rif) and feminine gender, in the sense of the tribe.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verse 69:

﴿And certainly Our messengers came to Ibrahim with the glad tidings﴾: they were Jibril, Mika'il and Israfil, or Jibril together with eleven angels. ﴿With the glad tidings﴾: this is the good news of a son, or of the destruction of the people of Lut. The first is more apparent. ﴿They said, "Peace."﴾: "We greet you with peace." ﴿He said, "Peace."﴾: "Your affair is peace." The reading "silm" (سِلْمٌ) is from Hamza and Ali, and it has the same meaning as salam (سَلامٌ). ﴿Then he did not delay in bringing a roasted calf﴾: "He did not delay in bringing it; rather, he hastened with it." Or: "his bringing it was not delayed." The calf (ʿijl, عِجْلٌ) is the young of a cow, and Ibrahim's wealth was cattle. ﴿Roasted﴾ (ḥanīdh, حَنِيذٍ): roasted over heated stones.

When he saw their hands not reaching toward the food, he regarded them with suspicion (nakirahum). Nakira and ankara (to disapprove, to be wary) carry the same meaning. It was their custom that if someone who came to them touched their food, they felt safe with him; otherwise they feared him. The apparent reading is that he sensed they were angels, and he was wary of them, because he feared that their coming was for a matter that God disapproved of, or to punish his people. The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿And he felt fear of them﴾, that is, he concealed fear of them. ﴿They said: Do not fear, for we have been sent to the people of Lot﴾ with punishment. This is said only to one who knows them and does not know for what purpose they were sent. They said "do not fear" because they saw the trace of fear and change in his face.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verse 71:

﴿And his wife was standing﴾ behind the screen, listening to their conversation, or standing over them, serving them. ﴿Then she laughed﴾ out of joy at the removal of fear, or at the destruction of the people of depravity, or at the heedlessness of the people of Lot despite the nearness of the punishment, or she menstruated. ﴿So We gave her good news of Isaac﴾, and she was singled out for the good news because women are greater in joy at a child than men, and because she had had no child while Abraham had a son, who was Ishmael. ﴿And after Isaac﴾, and after him, ﴿Jacob﴾. Ibn Amir, Hamzah and Hafs read it in the accusative (Ya'qub), by way of an implied verb indicated by what precedes it, meaning: "﴿So We gave her good news of Isaac﴾" (p-73), that is, "So We gave her good news of Isaac, and We granted her Jacob after Isaac." The others read it in the nominative (Ya'qub), as an inchoative, with the adverbial phrase preceding it as the predicate, just as you say "in the house is Zayd" (fi al-dar Zayd).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verse 72:

﴿She said, "Woe to me!"﴾ The alif (ا) is substituted for the ya' of possession (ياء الإضافة), and al-Hasan (al-Hasan al-Basri) read "يا ويلتي" (yā wailatī) with the ya' in its original form (على الأصل).

﴿Shall I give birth while I am an old woman?﴾ Daughter of ninety years.

﴿And this, my husband, is an old man﴾ Son of one hundred and twenty years. Here, "هذا" (hādhā, "this") is the subject (مبتدأ), "بعلي" (ba'lī, "my husband") is its predicate (خبر), and "شيخا" (shaykhan, "an old man") is a circumstantial accusative (حال). The element governing it (العامل) is either the sense of the demonstrative indicated by "ذا" (dhā), or the sense of the alerting exclamation indicated by "هذا" (hādhā).

﴿Indeed, this is a wondrous thing.﴾ That a child should be born to two such decrepit persons; this is an expression of astonishment (استبعاد) in terms of what is customary.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verse 73:

﴿They said: Do you wonder at the command of Allah?﴾ (i.e., at His power and His wisdom). The angels denied her wondering, because she was in the house of the signs (āyāt), the place of descent of miracles and matters that break the customary norms. So it was incumbent upon her to be dignified and not to be impressed by what impresses other women who grow up outside the house of prophethood, and to glorify and exalt Allah in place of wonder. The angels alluded to this when they said: ﴿The mercy of Allah and His blessings be upon you, O people of the house﴾, meaning: these and similar things are what the Lord of Majesty honours you with and singles you out to receive, O people of the house of prophethood. So it is not a strange matter. This is a resumed statement (kalām mustanaf) by which the denial of wonder is given its reason, as if it were said: Beware of wondering, for the likes of this mercy and blessing are abundant from Allah upon you. It has also been said: "the mercy" is prophethood, and "the blessings" are the tribes (asbāṭ) of the Children of Israel, because the prophets were among them, and they were all descendants of Ibrahim. "People of the house" is in the accusative either as a vocative (nidā') or by specification (ikhtisāṣ).

﴿Indeed, He is Praiseworthy﴾ (ḥamīd), worthy of praise for hastening favours; ﴿Glorious﴾ (majīd), manifestly generous in deferring retributions.

﴿When the fear had left Abraham﴾, meaning the fright, which is the apprehension he had felt because of the strangeness of his guests, ﴿and the good news had come to him﴾, namely of the son, ﴿he began to argue with Us concerning the people of Lot﴾. That is: when his heart was reassured after fear and he was filled with joy because of the good news, the fright (of the guests) departed from him, and he began to dispute. The answer to لَمّا (lamma, "when") is omitted, its estimated form being أقْبَلَ يُجادِلُنا ("he began to argue with Us"). Or يُجادِلُنا ("he argues with Us") is the answer to لَمّا, and it was brought in the present tense (يُجادِلُنا) for ḥikāyat al-ḥāl (the narration of a past state as if it were happening now, a grammatical device). The meaning is that he argued with Our messengers. His argument with them was that they said: ﴿Indeed, We are going to destroy the people of this town﴾ [al-ʿAnkabūt: 31]. He said: "Do you see, if there were fifty believers in it, would you destroy it?" They said: "No." He said: "Then forty?" They said: "No." He said: "Then thirty?" They said: "No," until he reached ten. They said: "No." He said: "Do you see, if there were in it one Muslim man, would you destroy it?" They said: "No." At that point ﴿he said: "Indeed, in it is Lot." They said: "We know best who is in it. We will surely save him and his family"﴾ [al-ʿAnkabūt: 32].

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verse 75:

﴿Indeed, Ibrahim was forbearing﴾, not hasty toward anyone who harmed him, or one who bore much patience toward those who hurt him, forgiving of those who disobeyed him. ﴿Awwah﴾: one who sighs much out of fear of Allah. ﴿Munib﴾: one who repents and returns to Allah. These attributes indicate tenderness of heart, compassion and mercy. Thus He explained that this is what moved him to plead with them, hoping that the punishment would be lifted from them and they would be given respite, so that perhaps they would turn in repentance, just as it moved him to seek forgiveness for his father.

"The angels said, ﴿O Ibrahim, turn away from this﴾ argument, even though compassion is your habit, ﴿for the command of your Lord has come﴾, that is, His decree and His judgment, ﴿and indeed there will come upon them a punishment that cannot be turned back﴾, that is, it cannot be averted by argument or by anything else. "Punishment" (ʿadhabun) is in the nominative by virtue of the active participle, and it is "āti-him" (coming to them); its estimated form is: "and indeed it will come to them."
